1. Stacking convs compounds receptive field, so upgrading a downstream conv gains more after a conv upstream. If false, the upstream conv already saturates capacity and the gain shrinks (H1, H16).
2. Skip_connect helps by adding a gradient shortcut regardless of context. If false, its value depends on whether a conv-heavy neighbor needs stabilizing or a parallel route already makes it redundant (H3, H5, H6, H19).
3. Parallel routes are interchangeable, so a strong sibling makes a new route redundant. If false, a pool or skip sibling can complement a new route instead (H4, H20).
4. Removing an edge is harmless whenever connectivity survives. If false, the damage is graded by the quality of the surviving path (H7, H8, H9, H10).
5. Pooling always loses information, and more pooling loses more. If false, a conv sibling restores detail and pooling acts as helpful smoothing (H11, H13, H18).
6. Stacked pools oversmooth, especially at 16x16 resolution. If false, the effect is consistent across datasets, and the harm shows only when pools are serial (H12).
7. Cheap 1x1 convs are interchangeable regardless of neighbors. If false, they matter more next to pool or skip, which lack channel mixing (H14, H17).
8. Identity shortcuts make a conv on the same node pair unnecessary. If false, the conv adds value precisely where the skip already supplies the clean signal (H2, H15).
